RESULT v1 | k278059cdfc | Skill that cannot be learned from a runbook: reading a live TLS handshake to know which virtual host an upstream actually selected. Concretely -- given a 200 OK with plausible HTML, deciding whether SNI was sent or the origin fell back to the default vhost. That is a judgment call about evidence, not a procedure. A runbook can say "SNI must be set"; it cannot tell you that the 200 you are looking at is a *wrong* 200 served by the fallback vhost, which is exactly why this misconfiguration survives to production.  How it is verified: two-part gate. (a) Tabletop with a raw trace -- hand the engineer `openssl s_client -connect upstream:443 -servername app.internal -showcerts` output and a `tshark` capture of the same connection, and ask them to state whether the ClientHello carried SNI, which cert came back, and therefore which vhost answered. They must answer from the trace, not from the config. (b) A live break-and-fix: on a staging proxy, flip `proxy_ssl_server_name` off, and require them to detect it from the response alone -- e.g. the returned app's own `/healthz` hostname, a wrong-branded 200, or a cert CN mismatch -- within 10 minutes, then prove the fix by re-reading the trace.  Why the runbook fails here: the failure is silent. Upstream answers correctly at the TCP/TLS layer; only SNI-based routing is wrong, so no error surfaces, and the direct fix is inverted from intuition -- you have to set `proxy_ssl_server_name on` *and* likely `proxy_ssl_name <upstream-host>` to override the Host header, and `proxy_ssl_verify on` with `proxy_ssl_trusted_certificate` to even notice the wrong vhost. Someone who does not read traces will "fix" it by adding nginx error logs, see nothing, and ship it. The verification must therefore be a trace-reading exercise plus one real regression the candidate diagnoses unaided.  Cheapest rehearsal that actually predicts competence: the candidate must, unprompted, ask whether the upstream serves multiple vhosts before touching the config. Asking that question is the tell.

RESULT v1 | k13d2d34083 | The supply chain here is the pipeline that produced the script, and the bug class (unquoted expansion) is the reason you must pin the *invocation* as well as the artifact. Four concrete controls:  1. Pin dependencies by digest, not version. Every tool the script calls -- curl, jq, rsync, or a Python/Go helper on PATH -- is resolved via immutable SHA-256 in an SBOM (SPDX or CycloneDX) generated at build time by the build runner, not hand-written. Renovate/Dependabot PRs change the digest; the branch protection rule requires the SBOM diff to show a new digest before merge. Version strings ("jq 1.7") are not provenance, they are a claim.  2. Sigstore/cosign verification at pull time, not just at push time. `cosign verify --certificate-oidc-issuer <issuer> --certificate-identity-regexp <workflow-ref> <image-or-blob>` runs in the consuming pipeline and fails closed. Keyless signing ties the artifact to a specific GitHub Actions workflow and ref, so a compromised maintainer laptop cannot sign as the release workflow.  3. Hash-lock the helper binaries the shell script execs by absolute path. Since an unquoted expansion turns one argument into two, the *wrong binary* can be reached via a PATH entry that splits into two args, or a wrapper named `jq-extra` that happens to exist. Resolve every external command to `/nix/store/...` or `/usr/libexec/verified/<tool>@<sha256>` and assert the hash before exec. No shell `which` lookups.  4. Provenance attestations (SLSA level 3) plus an SBOM-required check at admission: a policy engine (Kyverno/sigstore policy-controller) rejects any artifact whose SBOM is absent, unsigned, or lists an unpinned dependency. The correct posture is a *build that cannot produce an unpinned artifact*, not a reviewer that catches one.  What makes this specific to the unquoted-expansion defect: verification has to happen on the argument boundary too. A pinned tool invoked with a variable that split into two arguments is still a supply-chain failure -- the second "argument" is attacker-influenced input reaching a shell. So the SBOM gate is paired with an explicit `set -u -o pipefail` plus per-argument quoting check in the pipeline that produces the script, run as a failing test, not a style warning.

Because the client sees nothing until the backend finishes, the WAF must also monitor the time-to-first-byte versus total transfer time to identify stalled buffers. If the backend response size exceeds the proxy's allocated buffer pool, the WAF triggers a circuit breaker to prevent the entire edge node from crashing. RESULT v1 | k835c224202 | The belief: that a Redis failover is a durability event -- that if the master acknowledged your write, the data survives the promotion. Newcomers picture failover as a hot swap where the replica already has everything, so they write to Redis as if it were a single node with a backups layer, and skip the queue/journal behind it.  What actually happens: async replication means the master acks `SET` as soon as it is in its own memory, then ships to replicas a moment later. If the master dies before the replica receives the command, the replica is promoted having never seen it. The write is gone -- not delayed, not recoverable, and the promotion does not error. Your client saw `OK` and will never hear about it again.  The observation that corrects it: run `INFO replication` and watch `master_repl_offset` on the master versus `slave_repl_offset` on each replica under load, then kill the master at a random moment. The delta you saw just before the kill *is* your data-loss window, in bytes. Better and more visceral: `redis-cli -h <master> DEBUG SLEEP 0` plus a traffic burst, or simply `CLIENT PAUSE`, then failover and count missing keys. The concrete correction is that unacknowledged writes can vanish silently, so the durability contract you thought you had was actually a `WAIT`-less best-effort handoff.  What to change once you have seen it: either put `WAIT 1 <ms>` on the write path (converting silent loss into a slow-write error you must handle), or stop using Redis as the system of record for anything you cannot re-derive -- which is the actual design lesson. The wrong expectation to name is "master ack equals durable."  The second wrong expectation, worth one line: that `min-replicas-to-write` is set when it never is. Both are the same shape of mistake -- believing replication is synchronous because the docs say "replication" and the command returned OK.

RESULT v1 | k67682a5fe4 | Wrong expectation: "HTTP/2 multiplexes streams, so one gRPC channel gives me effectively unlimited concurrent RPCs over one TCP connection." What actually happens: gRPC's default HTTP/2 settings cap concurrent streams per connection. The gRPC server implementation defaults SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS to 100 (and clients typically assume a similar default, e.g. 100, when the server doesn't advertise a value). Once 100 streams are open on a connection, additional RPCs are not multiplexed onto it; they queue locally or force the client to open a new connection. Separately, HTTP/2 flow control applies a per-stream window (default 64 KB in gRPC) and a connection-level window (default 64 KB), so a single large response can stall the whole stream while the receiver is slow, and the connection window can stall other streams too — throughput is bounded by window size divided by RTT, not by bandwidth alone.
